title: Fallen Is Babylon: The Watchman's Oracles
summary: Three short oracles share the image of a watchman waiting for news. In the first, the prophet sees a terrifying vision of Elam and Media attacking the Desert by the Sea, and a lookout finally reports: fallen, fallen is Babylon. In the second, someone calls from Seir asking how much of the night is left, and the watchman gives a cryptic reply. In the third, Arabian caravans and refugees flee the sword, and the glory of Kedar is to end within a year.
story: Babylon returns. The collection of oracles against the nations began with Babylon (chapter 13), and chapter 21 announces its fall again, this time through the eyes of a shaken prophet who feels the vision in his body. Then the oracles move to the peoples of the desert east and south of Judah: Dumah and Seir, linked with Edom, and the Arabian oases and tribes of Dedan, Tema, and Kedar. The chapter is full of waiting and watching, which suits its place in the book: Judah is a people crushed on the threshing floor (verse 10), waiting to learn whether any power can rescue it. The next chapter will turn the same searching gaze on Jerusalem itself.
historical:
The Desert by the Sea is a riddling title for Babylon, which lay in the flat lands of southern Mesopotamia near the marshes and the head of the Persian Gulf; Assyrian texts call the region nearest the gulf the Sealand. Elam lay east of Babylonia, and Media northeast of it. Which fall of Babylon is meant is debated. Many scholars link it to Cyrus the Persian's capture of Babylon in 539 BC, since the Persians came from the old Elamite region of Anshan and ruled the Medes, and the feasting princes of verse 5 recall the feast of Belshazzar on the night Babylon fell (Daniel 5). Others place it in Isaiah's own time, when Babylon under Merodach-baladan rebelled against Assyria with Elamite support and fell to Sargon II around 710 BC and to Sennacherib in 689 BC. On this reading, the command to Elam and Media may be understood differently, and the fall of Babylon would have dashed the hopes of those in Judah who saw it as an ally against Assyria (compare Isaiah 39).

Dumah was an oasis in northern Arabia, probably modern Dumat al-Jandal, and Seir is the mountain country of Edom, south of the Dead Sea. Dedan (near modern al-Ula) and Tema (modern Tayma) were oasis towns on the caravan routes of northwest Arabia, and Kedar was a powerful confederation of Arab tribes in the Syrian and Arabian desert. Assyrian kings campaigned against Arab tribes repeatedly, including Sargon II and Sennacherib, and later the Babylonian king Nabonidus lived at Tema for about ten years in the sixth century BC.
cultural:
City walls and watchtowers were manned day and night by lookouts who reported approaching riders or armies. News of distant events traveled by runners and mounted messengers, and a lookout might watch for days before anything came. Verse 7 lists the transport of a mixed army: chariots with horses, and riders on donkeys and camels. Oiling the shields (verse 5) was a preparation for battle, keeping leather shields supple, and the command comes abruptly in the middle of a feast.

Desert life depended on hospitality. Caravans of the Dedanites carried goods such as incense and spices along the Arabian trade routes, camping at oases. Refugees fleeing an army needed water and bread, and verse 14 calls on the people of Tema to meet them with food, the basic duty of desert peoples toward travelers in distress. The archers of Kedar were famous, and the glory of Kedar refers to its wealth in flocks and its military strength.
literary: Each of the three oracles begins with a burden heading (verses 1, 11, and 13), and each uses a cryptic title: the Desert by the Sea, Dumah (which means silence, possibly a wordplay on Edom), and Arabia (which can also mean evening or steppe). The first oracle is unusually personal: the prophet describes physical anguish, confusion, and fear at what he sees (verses 3 and 4). The central scene is dramatic, with God commanding a lookout, the lookout reporting his long watch, and the climactic cry: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon.” The Dumah oracle is only two verses, a haunting exchange of question and answer about the night. The Arabia oracle ends with a precise timetable like 16:14, within one year as a hired worker would count it.

outline.t: A dire vision against the Desert by the Sea and the prophet's anguish
The lookout's report: fallen, fallen is Babylon
The oracle on Dumah: watchman, what is left of the night?
The oracle on Arabia: refugees, caravans, and the end of Kedar's glory

doctrines.note: Babylon's fall includes the shattering of the images of her gods. God's judgment on an empire is also the exposure of the gods it trusted.
The prophet receives a vision he did not want and cannot control, and it grips him with anguish. God's word is given, not invented, and the prophet reports what he has heard from the LORD of Hosts.
The watchman's answer that morning comes, but also the night, holds hope and warning together. Relief may come, yet darkness is not finished, and the questioner is invited to keep asking.

words.note: Tsaphah, to watch or keep lookout. It describes the lookout posted in verse 6. The prophets often describe themselves as watchmen, responsible to see danger and warn the people (Ezekiel 3:17, Habakkuk 2:1).

Naphal, to fall. The doubled cry of verse 9, fallen, fallen, uses it for Babylon, and it describes the images of her gods lying shattered on the ground. The repetition gives the news the finality of a death announcement.

Baah, to inquire or ask, a rare verb (it is Aramaic-like in form, and appears twice in verse 12). The watchman's reply, if you would inquire, then inquire, leaves the door open: the questioner may come back and ask again.

Qedar, Kedar, a people descended in Genesis from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13) and a byword for the Arab tribes of the desert. The Old Testament mentions their tents, flocks, and archers. Their glory ending within a year shows that desert strength was no more secure than city walls.

christ: The cry of verse 9 is taken up in the book of Revelation, where an angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen (Revelation 14:8 and 18:2). There Babylon stands for every proud power opposed to God and his people, and its fall is part of the victory of the Lamb. Isaiah's first horizon is a real historical fall of Babylon; Revelation reads that event as a pattern of what Christ will finally do to every empire that sets itself against God. The Dumah oracle's question about the night also resonates with the New Testament's picture of Christians as people who live in the night but belong to the day, watching for its coming (Romans 13:12, 1 Thessalonians 5:4-8).

hard.q: Which fall of Babylon does this chapter describe, and why does it matter?
hard.a: Scholars disagree. One view links the chapter to 539 BC, when Cyrus, ruling the Medes and coming from the Elamite region, took Babylon, and notes the parallel with Belshazzar's feast in Daniel 5. Those who hold this view differ over whether Isaiah foresaw it from the eighth century or whether the oracle comes from a later prophet in the Isaiah tradition. Another view places it in Isaiah's own lifetime, when Babylon fell to Assyria in about 710 BC or 689 BC, and argues that the prophet's distress in verses 3 and 4 makes more sense if Babylon's fall was bad news for Judah, which had hoped in Babylon's resistance to Assyria. Each view accounts for some details better than others. The chapter's message is the same on either reading: the gods of Babylon cannot save it, and the people of God, crushed on the threshing floor, must look to the LORD of Hosts.

questions: The prophet is shaken by what God shows him. Why might an honest response to God's word sometimes be distress rather than calm?
Watchman, what is left of the night? When have you asked a question like that, and what did waiting teach you?
The people of Tema are told to meet refugees with bread and water. Who are the refugees on your road, and what would it mean to meet them?
